Biryar can decide what each of your listings should cost, explain why,
and — once you switch it on — change the price on Amazon.

It is off. A listing arrives unmanaged, and an install arrives unable
to change a price at all. Both are deliberate: the whole catalogue
being repriced the moment Amazon is connected is the one default that
cannot be taken back.

## What it does on a pass

Every hour, for each listing you have turned on:

1. Reads the market — who else is selling it, for how much including
   delivery, and who currently holds the Featured Offer.
2. Decides which of four situations the listing is in, and what band
   of prices that situation allows.
3. Picks a price inside the band.
4. Writes down what it decided and why — including when it decided to
   change nothing, which is most of the time on a healthy catalogue.
5. Submits the price, if it is allowed to.

## The floor

No price goes below it, ever. It is the higher of two numbers:

- **Break-even**, measured from your own settled transactions — not a
  fee schedule, not an estimate. What Amazon actually took from your
  last sales, as a rate plus a flat charge per unit.
- **Your own minimum** in Seller Central. Amazon refuses to publish
  outside it anyway, including from its own automated pricing.

Which of the two bound is recorded with every decision, because they
call for opposite responses. "This would lose money" is a fact about
the product. "Your Seller Central minimum forbids it" is a setting you
can change in a minute — and a refusal that misnames its own cause
argues against its own fix.

A listing with no minimum or maximum in Seller Central cannot be
repriced at all. Biryar will not invent one: that is the single number
you are entitled to decide.

## What stops it

**The day, not the step.** Every single move is clamped, so no one
decision can be large. What can run away is a day of them — five per
cent a pass, many passes, is a price anywhere at all. So the gate is
cumulative: once a listing has moved more than 8% from its first price
of the day, the next move waits for you. The counter is read from the
journal, not held in memory, so restarting Biryar does not reset it.

**A price already on its way.** Amazon takes ten minutes and more to
publish a submission, and a pass reads the *published* price — still
the old one meanwhile. Without a guard the same target is re-derived
and re-sent every pass until it lands. A SKU with a submission less
than 45 minutes old is left alone.

**The writer itself.** It re-checks the floor and ceiling immediately
before submitting, after the policy already has. The facts the policy
used were read minutes ago, and this is the last code that runs before
a price is public.

## Approving is not publishing

When the daily gate stops a move, approving it marks the decision and
nothing else. The next pass re-reads the market and works out a
current price.

That is on purpose. An approval given this morning, for a figure
computed last night, is an instruction about an intention rather than
about a number — a competitor can move in between, and publishing the
stale figure would obey the letter of your approval against its
purpose. One approval lets one move through.

## Switching it on

Three things, and you decide all of them.

**Per listing**, on the Repricing page: tick the ones Biryar may
touch. Off until you say otherwise.

**The plan.** Sending prices is part of Pro. On the free plan every
pass still runs when you ask: it decides, explains, writes down, and
asks Amazon to validate, and nothing is applied. That is a preview of
exactly what Pro would do. See [Plans](/plans/).

**The switch**, under Settings, Repricing. Owner-only, and off until
the owner turns it on, with what it means written beside it: from then
on Biryar changes prices on Amazon while nobody is watching.

Until all three are in place everything still runs: the pass decides,
records, and asks Amazon to *validate* each submission without applying
it. So you can watch exactly what would happen, against your real
catalogue and real competitors, before anything does. Every decision
from that period reads `would have changed, not live`.

**How often** is on the same page: every 15 minutes, every hour, every
four hours, once a day. A pass can also be started at any time from the
Repricing page, and the page shows it running: the catalogue being read
from Amazon, then each listing being priced.

## Seeing what it did

The Repricing card shows the journal, decisions that changed nothing
included. A screen that listed only changes would look identical on a
quiet day and a broken one. While the learner is watching, each line
also says what it would have charged instead, and the Learning section
totals those up: how often it disagreed, by how much, and how often it
sat at an end of the band.

From a terminal:

```bash
python -m biryar.catalogue --refresh   # what is listed, and its bounds
python -m biryar.reprice               # what it would charge, and why
```

Neither writes anything to Amazon. `reprice` is the preview: it reads
the live market and prints the decision for every priceable listing
without recording or submitting it. Each line carries the learner's
own number too, and the header says which stage it is at — so a figure
it would charge is never mistaken for one that would be published.

The learner's number is a draw from what it believes, not a fixed
answer, so two previews of one listing differ. What is worth reading
off a run of them is whether it clusters at one end of the band, not
any single price.

## Learning where to sit in the band

Steps 2 and 3 of a pass are different in kind. Deciding the band is a
rule — four situations, each with a floor and a ceiling, and you can
read it and disagree with it. Picking a price *inside* that band is a
guess, and the rule's guess is the middle, which is a reasonable thing
to do and not a measured one.

So there is a second chooser, and it learns that part from your own
sales.

### What it learns

Five positions in the band: at the floor, a quarter of the way up, the
middle, three quarters, at the ceiling. It holds one position for a
few days, counts what sold, and works out the profit per day that
position returned. Over time it comes to prefer the positions that
earned the most on *your* catalogue, and keeps trying the others
occasionally in case the market moved.

It learns positions rather than prices on purpose. A price means
nothing next week once the competition has moved; "three quarters of
the way up whatever band I am allowed" survives. It is also why it
cannot be unsafe: a position is inside the band, and the band is what
keeps the floor. The worst a wrong position can do is leave money on
the table — it cannot sell below cost, because there is no position
that addresses a price the rule refused.

### It starts knowing something

A learner starting from nothing explores at random, and on a
catalogue selling a few units a day that is months of paying for
information. So Biryar ships with a measured starting belief about
each of the five positions, taken from graded experiments on a real
account.

It is weak on purpose — worth about four of your own experiments, and
then your evidence outvotes it. A strong shipped belief would be this
product telling you that what worked on somebody else's account works
on yours, which is not a claim it can make. It carries three numbers
per position and nothing else: no prices, no SKUs, no competitors, no
identifiers.

### It does not price anything until you say so

A repricer cannot be tested the way a classifier can. A classifier's
shadow run is a real test, because the right answer arrives whatever
predicted it. A pricing policy's shadow run is not: the units sold
belong to the price that was actually *published*, and a shadow's
price never is. So it moves through three stages, and each answers a
different question.

| Stage | What it does | What it can tell you |
|---|---|---|
| **Watching** | Records the price it would have chosen. Publishes nothing. | Whether it is sane — does it disagree with the rule, by how much, and has it pinned itself to one edge of the band. Costs nothing. It *cannot* tell you whether it earns more, and no amount of waiting will change that. |
| **Pricing part of the catalogue** | Prices some of your listings; the rule prices the rest. | Whether it earns more. This is a measurement. Everything before it is an estimate. |
| **Pricing everything** | Prices all of them. | — |

The trial splits by listing, not by week: alternating weeks would
confound the comparison with whatever else moved that week — a
competitor's stockout, a season, a fee change. The split is worked out
from each SKU's own name, so it survives a restart and you can
recompute it yourself.

**Nothing promotes itself.** The Repricing card reports whether the
evidence would support the next stage, and why not when it would not.
Moving it is a button you press, recorded as your decision. A pricing
policy that moved itself into production on its own assessment of its
own performance is precisely the arrangement this is built to prevent.

The report is advice and not a lock: you can go straight to pricing
everything, or back to watching after a bad week, without arguing with
a threshold.

### Why it may say nothing for a while

Three things have to be true before an experiment counts, and when
they are not, the honest answer is that there is no evidence yet.

- **The price has to sit still long enough.** The profit is divided by
  the days it was held, so a price replaced after twenty minutes would
  turn one sale into seventy units a day. Anything held less than half
  a day is thrown away rather than fed in as noise.
- **The cost has to be known.** A listing with no purchase cost
  recorded is skipped, not graded as though the goods were free.
- **The market has to leave it alone.** On a listing where the
  competition moves every hour, no price is ever held long enough to
  grade, and nothing is learned about it. That is a true description
  of what is knowable there, not a fault.

Which is also why watching, on its own, never becomes enough: the
experiments it grades are the rule's prices, not its own.
